Agents inspect content, verify requests, and execute actions in simulated applications, with attack outcomes grounded in verifiable tool execution logs. To enable controlled red teaming of personal agents, we design a multimodal attack harness that integrates task information, attack progression control, and multimodal content construction to evaluate their intrinsic security against adaptive social engineering attacks in simulated environments. Evaluating seven widely used multimodal models across six dimensions reveals that all are vulnerable, with attack success rates of 7.1% to 34.5%. Adding multimodal content increases attack success from 19.9% to 29.2%, despite increased proactive verification coverage. Stronger safety instructions reduce attack success without improving recognition of deceptive multimodal content, while lower attack success rates for some models accompany excessive refusal of legitimate requests.

papers.title: Dynamical Keldysh model for colored noise and finite relaxation rate
papers.summary: The Keldysh model describes quantum dots subjected to Gaussian noise with infinite correlation time. For multi-component noise coupled through non-commuting matrices, the spectrum exhibits a pseudogap. We solve the model for coloured noise with any correlation time, $1/ γ$. Finite memory leads to the pseudogap being filled, its peaks merging and the line narrowing.

papers.title: Has Quarkyonic Matter Been Seen in Lattice Simulations?
papers.summary: Quarkyonic Matter refers to the dual state of matter between confined hadrons and quasi-free quarks. This duality leads to a robust constraint on the behavior of the distribution functions. After a comprehensive review of Quarkyonic Matter based on the distribution functions, we discuss recent lattice data for two-color QCD in $(1+1)$ and $(3+1)$ dimensions at finite baryon number density and QCD in $(3+1)$ dimensions at finite isospin density, as well as the astrophysically inferred equation of state. Taken together, these results reveal a coherent picture consistent with the emergence of Quarkyonic Matter in lattice simulations. Future lattice calculations of baryon and gauge-invariant quark momentum distributions at high density would provide a more direct test of this interpretation.

papers.title: Construction and performance evaluation of a meter-scale monolithic scintillator tracker with embedded scatterers
papers.summary: A meter-scale Fiber-Readout mOnolithic and Scatterer-embedded scintillator Tracker (FROST) was constructed and operated in the NINJA experiment to enable muon-track matching between the nuclear emulsion detectors and the downstream muon detector. The detector consists of a 1.32 m $\times$ 1.40 m plastic scintillator plate assembled from optically bonded scatterer-embedded plates, with wavelength-shifting fibers arranged at a pitch of 10 mm. During J-PARC neutrino-beam operation, FROST achieved a data acquisition efficiency of 99.59% and a detection efficiency of 99.946$\pm$0.006% for selected neutrino-induced muons well within the active area. A position reconstruction method based on the light-yield distribution was developed for both single- and multi-particle events. In a neutrino-interaction simulation, muon position resolutions of 1.77 mm and 1.61 mm were achieved in the two orthogonal readout directions, assuming correct muon identification. Using a beam-data sample dominated by single-muon events, upper limits on the position resolution of 2.20 mm and 2.03 mm were obtained for track angles below 20°. These results demonstrate that the FROST concept can be scaled up to a meter-scale active area while maintaining high detection efficiency and a position resolution well below the readout pitch under actual experimental conditions.
papers.comment: 37 pages, 17 figures. Submitted to Nuclear Instruments and Methods in Physics Research Section A

papers.title: LeanContext: Disentangling Mathematical Resources from Local Formal Context in Lean Whole-Proof Generation
papers.summary: Neural theorem proving increasingly uses retrieved premises and project context to support proof generation. Evaluating these resources requires measuring the advantage of target-selected declarations over comparable alternatives and how this advantage depends on training. We introduce LeanContext, a benchmark of 129,826 Lean whole-proof generation problems, to investigate these questions. We group selected complete preceding mathematical declarations as Mathematical Context (MC) and the remaining selected local source commands as Environment Context (EC). Four aligned input views support crossed training and inference evaluations with shared targets and original Lean verification environments. For both diffusion- and autoregressive-based models, selected declarations outperform comparable alternatives by a larger margin when training includes MC. Final-input audits identify omitted declarations referenced by the target. Prioritizing these dependencies improves Pass@32 by 1.40% and 1.70% for LLaDA and Llama, respectively, on 2,000 targets. The selection experiment operates without access to target reference proofs and holds checkpoints, EC, and inference budgets constant. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/haaaardcvZ/LeanContext.

papers.title: Aligning Policy Encoders with a Shape Teacher
papers.summary: 3D-aware representations can improve robotic manipulation by providing geometric information that is robust to changes in viewpoint, object position, and occlusion. However, using 3D inputs at deployment requires additional sensing and processing, making image-based policies more practical. We ask whether an image-based policy can acquire 3D shape information during training while retaining a purely image-based interface at deployment. We propose shape-teacher alignment, a training-time mechanism that uses a pretrained 3D shape representation as an alignment target for an image-based policy encoder. Specifically, we use Point-MAE features from individual objects as targets for corresponding image patches, transferring geometric structure to the policy without changing its deployment inputs or architecture. On LIBERO, shape-teacher alignment produces image representations that are more structured around object shape and corresponding parts, while substantially accelerating policy convergence and improving success rates. For pretrained policies, convergence is accelerated by 4.7x and 5.6x on the Object and Spatial suites, respectively, without requiring the shape teacher or depth input at deployment.

papers.title: Wireless Link Scheduling with Graph Signal Diffusion
papers.summary: We solve long-horizon wireless link scheduling with per-link minimum transmission constraints. Fair distribution of resources across links and time steps requires stochastic scheduling, motivating a diffusion framework. Via imitation learning, we train a diffusion model to sample scheduling decisions, conditioning generation on the network topology and constraint levels. The parameterization is achieved through a U-Graph Neural Network (U-GNN) to leverage the relationship between graphs and wireless networks for learning. Our approach achieves near-optimal performance, maximizing sum rate while distributing allocations across different links over time horizons. The U-GNN-based diffusion model generalizes to requirements and network sizes unseen during training, demonstrating the robustness of the approach.

papers.title: Analytic parametrisations of the scale dependence of proton parton distributions
papers.summary: Parton distribution functions (PDFs) are non-perturbative inputs whose scale dependence is governed by the Dokshitzer-Gribov-Lipatov-Altarelli-Parisi (DGLAP) equations. Their numerical evaluation commonly relies on interpolation of tabulated grids. We discuss an analytic representation of collinear proton PDFs in $(x,Q^2)$, obtained by promoting the parameters of a standard $x$-space parametrisation to functions of the scale. The coefficients are reconstructed from the HERAPDF2.0 NLO set using machine-assisted fitting techniques, with sampling in $10^{-4}\le x\le 0.65$ and scales up to 1 TeV. The resulting ML-PDFs reproduce integrated distributions at the sub-percent level for most flavours, with deviations reaching about 1.5% for the strange quark at the highest scales. They satisfy valence and momentum sum rules at the percent level and reproduce representative $pp\toπ$ and $pp\toγπ$ cross sections within approximately 2% and 5%, respectively, in the kinematic regions studied. Compared with grid interpolation through LHAPDF, direct evaluation of the analytic expressions reduces the total Monte Carlo run time by about 11% and 30% in these two applications.
papers.comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 1 table, contribution to the proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on High Energy Physics (ICHEP 2026), 30 July - 5 August 2026, Natal, Brazil

papers.title: DART: Domain-Agnostic Residual Transfer for Generalist Anomaly Detection
papers.summary: Generalist Anomaly Detection (GAD) aims to detect anomalies in unseen domains using only a few reference samples. Recent normal-abnormal guided methods improve this setting by exploiting abnormal references, but their residuals often mix transferable anomaly cues with domain-specific appearance factors such as texture, geometry, and acquisition conditions. This residual domain entanglement limits cross-domain transfer and may produce spurious activations on novel domains. We propose DART, a plug-in framework for normal-abnormal guided GAD that learns to separate residuals into anomaly-relevant and domain-specific components. DART combines a Residual Disentanglement Module, which preserves anomaly-discriminative information while suppressing domain information, with Cross-Domain Meta-Training, which forms episodes across source domains to make the separation effective. The method is architecture-agnostic and can be inserted between residual computation and the detection head of existing GAD pipelines. Experiments on MVTec AD, VisA, and BraTS show consistent improvements over multiple base methods, with the largest gains under stronger domain shifts. https://github.com/aqeeelmirza/DART

papers.title: Spin supersolid in triangular lattice easy-axis spin-1/2 antiferromagnet: a fermionic parton perspective
papers.summary: We study the supersolid order of the spin-1/2 easy-axis XXZ antiferromagnet on the triangular lattice using a fermionic parton mean-field theory built on the $π$-flux Dirac spin liquid, with the mean-field order generated by an on-site spinon interaction term and nearest-neighbor (anisotropic) spin couplings. The collective modes are obtained using the random-phase approximation (RPA). In a finite parameter region, we find the Y state as a self-consistent solution, together with the competing Y' state, which is a $90^\circ$-rotated Y state inside the order plane. The mean-field energy favors Y', even though the two states are exactly degenerate in the classical limit. However, the Y state can become lower in energy when higher-order corrections due to the fluctuations of the collective modes are considered. The Y state can also be stabilized on the mean-field level by applying small external fields, which we do in two different ways: moment-aligned local field and uniform field along the easy axis. In both cases, the RPA calculation for the stabilized Y state gives a roton minimum at the $M$ point in the excitation spectrum. A gapped pseudo-Goldstone mode above the gapless Goldstone mode is obtained as well, which has also been observed experimentally. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of tuning the spinon interaction strength and the anisotropy in spin couplings in our phenomenological model. Comparison with the recent numerical and experimental results is also discussed.

papers.title: The slower rotation of planet-hosting stars revisited
papers.summary: Previous studies combined rotation periods derived from Kepler photometry, stellar parameters from previous Gaia Data Releases, and planet hosts from the NASA Exoplanet Archive to conclude that statistically planet-hosting stars rotate slower than stars without detected planets. Here, we revisit these studies by using similar Kepler rotational period sample, but with an updated Gaia DR3-based stellar parameter catalogue and an updated exoplanet catalogue. We apply minimal sample cuts in evolutionary state, metallicity, and distance, and then model the stellar rotation period as a function of effective temperature alone. For each star, we derive the ratio of its observed period to the temperature-expected period, and compare the ratio distributions for the planet-host and non-host stars. For periods shorter than 20 d, the planet-host distribution of this ratio is shifted towards longer periods; the period-ratio median is ~15% larger for hosts than for non-hosts (p_KS = 2.4 x 10^-4). We also examine the recently published TESS All-Sky Rotation Survey (TARS) and find a similar trend. However, the strongly structured period distribution precludes a robust comparison between the host and the non-host stars. Therefore, the updated analysis, using more robust stellar and planetary parameters, recovers the previously reported association, strengthening the case for a genuine connection between stellar rotation and planet occurrence.
papers.comment: 4 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for publication in MNRAS

papers.title: The index of mesoscopic Wilson--Dirac operators: I
papers.summary: This is the first of a series of papers which will be devoted to a study of the index of mesoscopic Wilson--Dirac operators on closed Riemannian manifolds. The aim of the series is to discretise the index of the Dirac operator. On flat tori, this is achieved by the Wilson--Dirac operator of lattice gauge theory on a regular lattice. On a general closed Riemannian manifold, however, no regular lattice is available. As an intermediate step between the continuum Dirac operator and its discretisations, we introduce mesoscopic Wilson--Dirac operators on any closed Riemannian manifold, defined by integrating covariant differences over distances comparable to a fixed length scale. In this paper, we define the index of the mesoscopic Wilson--Dirac operators via spectral flow and prove that it agrees with that of the continuum Dirac operator at all sufficiently small scales. The proof rests on an elliptic estimate uniform in the scale and a Rellich-type compactness theorem. In the second paper, we shall pass from mesoscopic operators to discrete Wilson--Dirac operators.

papers.title: SplatAnything: Gaussian Spacing Normalization for Feed-forward 3DGS across Arbitrary Scenes
papers.summary: We identify a key limitation of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods: Gaussian attributes are typically predicted in a radial-distance-normalized space that canonicalizes a global radial statistic of the reconstructed geometry, while the spacing between neighboring Gaussian centers can still vary substantially across scene scales and camera configurations. This mismatch induces systematic shifts in Gaussian-scale targets, leading to ambiguous supervision. To address this, we propose SplatAnything with Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm), which canonicalizes a robust scene-level statistic of Gaussian spacing to provide a more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian prediction. To rigorously assess our method, we further establish a systematic benchmark spanning diverse datasets, input sparsity levels, and challenging extrapolated viewpoints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SplatAnything achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong gains under substantial variations in scene scale and viewpoint.

papers.title: The Geometry of Simulated Perspectives: Dissociating Representation and Behaviour in a Multimodal Language Model
papers.summary: Multimodal language models can simulate different observers, yet it remains unclear how assigned perspectives reshape their internal representations and whether these changes govern their judgements. Here, we investigate the representational geometry of persona-conditioned visual interestingness in Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct. Across 100 images and 53 prompting conditions, we systematically vary persona content and the linguistic framing used to introduce it, while recording behavioural ratings and layer-wise hidden states. We observe a systematic reorganisation of representational geometry across processing depth: early layers primarily encode image identity, whereas persona-specific structures emerge in later layers. Strikingly, prompt framing reshapes internal representations more strongly than persona identity, whereas persona content has a greater impact on behavioural judgements. This dissociation is further illustrated by minimal identity statements that alter representations even without changing responses. These findings demonstrate that representational distance does not necessarily reflect behavioural relevance. More broadly, they reveal how simulated perspectives emerge as distinct structures within the representational space of artificial cognitive systems, highlighting a fundamental distinction between the geometry of internal representations and their functional consequences.
papers.comment: 30 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Code: https://github.com/MathisImm/persona-vlm-representations; data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23664820

papers.title: A characteristic mapping method for dissipative evolution equations
papers.summary: The Characteristic Mapping (CM) method is a transport scheme which discretizes the Lagrangian flow map as a composition of spatial interpolants. This adaptive approximation technique has demonstrated novel resolution properties and the ability to efficiently simulate the fine scales of inviscid turbulent flows. In this work, we construct an extension of this approach to the solution of dissipative problems, including the Navier-Stokes equations. The extension lifts a general scalar evolution equation to a path in a group of diffeomorphisms, where the semigroup approach of the CM method can be exploited. We give an interpretation of this lift through the geometric framework of optimal transport. We then introduce a semidirect product evolution technique to perform the time stepping of the map components. The map is evolved based on the semi-Lagrangian CM approach, and its log-Jacobian is evolved explicitly by an exponential integrator. The numerical scheme is demonstrated to be high-order accurate and is tested on a range of canonical nonlinear dissipative equations. By retaining the resolution properties of the CM method, the approach shows a promising ability to simulate turbulent fluid flows across all Reynolds numbers.

papers.title: Fault-Geometry-Aware Control Allocation for Emergency Quadrotor Landing under Single-Motor Loss of Effectiveness
papers.summary: Partial single-motor loss of effectiveness (LoE) changes the remaining control-authority geometry of a quadrotor and can change which control allocator performs best during emergency landing[cite: 11]. We compare three allocators in Crazyflie software-in-the-loop simulation: bounded weighted least squares (reported as PINV), a finite-candidate residual allocator (QP-lite), and the same residual allocator with scoring parameters tuned offline by the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM)[cite: 11]. For this study, fault geometry is represented by the known failed-motor index[cite: 11]. At $η=0.496$ remaining effectiveness, matched development trials select CEM for M1, M3, and M4 and PINV for M2; the M3 selection is a one-trial margin (29/30 versus 28/30)[cite: 11]. After freezing this routing map, the policy achieves 117/120 safe first-contact touchdowns on fresh seeds and 115/120 in a separate randomized-order integrated-supervisor evaluation[cite: 11]. For the critical M2/PINV branch, Firth regression gives a nominal $η_{50}\approx0.4956$ with a within-model 95% bootstrap interval of approximately [0.4955, 0.4956][cite: 11]. One-factor-at-a-time $\pm10\%$ plant perturbations shift $η_{50}$ by up to 0.05495 for thrust coefficient and 0.04974 for mass; the most frequent violated first-contact criterion also changes from vertical speed in many conditions to angular rate for mass -10% and thrust-coefficient +10%[cite: 11]. At fixed $η=0.496$, PINV has a higher M2 safe count than frozen CEM in 9/11 tested plant states and ties in 2/11; the two ties are both 0/30[cite: 11]. The experiments therefore distinguish motor-conditioned allocator selection from sensitivity to plant-model mismatch[cite: 11].

papers.title: Thermodynamics of Forgetting in a Bounded Hopfield Network
papers.summary: A memory that keeps learning must also forget. The Hopfield network does not: beyond a critical number of stored patterns it falls into a state of total confusion and retrieves none of them. Parisi showed in 1986 that bounding the synaptic strength cures this pathology, since the clipping of the couplings gradually erases the oldest memories and leaves room for the new ones. In this paper we provide a thermodynamic description of the resulting network, known as the Hopfield-Parisi model. Starting from the learning rule, we show that the network is equivalent to a Hopfield model whose patterns are weighted according to their age, superimposed on a Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass, both governed by the synaptic bound: a larger bound makes the memory longer, but also noisier. The theory of nonlinear networks developed in the eighties already provides, through the heuristic replica method, the equations that govern this model at any temperature, but to the best of our knowledge they have been solved only at zero temperature. We rederive them at the replica symmetric level through Guerra's interpolation and solve them at finite temperature, obtaining the phase diagram of the model together with its memory horizon, namely the largest age at which a pattern can still be retrieved. The solution shows that forgetting acts on the signal alone, the noise being the same for patterns of every age, and that the horizon is maximal at an intermediate bound which is essentially insensitive to temperature. Monte Carlo simulations of networks trained with the original learning rule support these predictions.

papers.title: Entropic measures of quantum information
papers.summary: Entropy has played a pivotal role in physics ever since its inception by Clausius in the early industrial age. Shannon ushered the concept into the information age by using it to describe fundamental limits of information processing, founding the field of information theory. Today, a fruitful interaction between information theory and physics is pushing our understanding of entropy forward. It has revealed, in particular, that no single notion of entropy suffices to capture all relevant properties of physical systems, making it necessary to consider a variety of entropic measures of quantum information, each with distinct features and uses. This review surveys these recent advances in a structured way, covering a comprehensive array of information measures, including Rényi and smooth entropies, together with their interrelations. Starting with a systematic characterization of entropies that motivates their definitions from natural physical principles, we discuss their applications ranging from quantum communication and cryptography to resource theories, thermodynamics, and many-body physics.
papers.comment: 84-page review article. Comments and suggestions very welcome

papers.title: VoxCanvas-41M: A Large-Scale Bilingual Dataset for Instruction-Based Speech Editing and Its Learning Dynamics
papers.summary: Recent advances in speech generation have spurred the development of speech editing techniques. However, achieving high-quality speech editing remains challenging due to two key limitations. First, the major hurdle is the lack of large-scale, high-quality speech editing datasets. Constructing such datasets is costly, while open-source, scalable data pipelines remain limited. Second, the learning dynamics of speech editing models remain poorly understood. In particular, how models acquire editing capabilities and the relationship between generation and editing remain unclear. To address these challenges, we introduce VoxCanvas-41M, a large-scale bilingual dataset comprising approximately 41 million speech editing pairs. VoxCanvas-41M covers two major categories: content editing, including single-span, multi-span, and location-reference editing, and paralinguistic editing, covering the insertion and deletion of 39 classes of nonverbal events such as laughter, sighs, and coughs. Building on VoxCanvas-41M, we train VoxCanvas-Edit, an instruction-based speech editing model, demonstrating the effectiveness of our dataset in improving editing performance. Furthermore, we systematically investigate the learning dynamics of speech editing, examining how models learn different editing operations and how data scale, task interactions, and training strategies affect editing performance. The dataset, pipeline, and demos are publicly available.

papers.title: Finite-element reconstruction of molten-zone dynamics and chemical segregation in optical floating-zone grown Ni--Mn--Ga
papers.summary: Homogeneous single-crystal growth of Ni--Mn--Ga magnetic shape-memory alloys is limited by incongruent melting, Mn reactivity, and longitudinal composition segregation. We report a modified optical floating-zone method in which growth is performed inside a transparent sapphire crucible, stabilising the molten zone while preserving optical heating and visual monitoring. The resulting crystals show improved growth reproducibility and controlled macroscopic geometry. To interpret the measured segregation profiles, a transient finite-element heat-transfer model in COMSOL Multiphysics was coupled to an effective molten-zone mass-balance calculation. The model reveals that the local solidification velocity is not fixed by the imposed translation speed but varies strongly as the molten-zone geometry evolves. The calculated solidification-front geometry is independently supported by EBSD analysis of a quenched growth interface, while the coupled mass-balance calculation reproduces the dominant features of the measured composition profiles. These results show that deviations from ideal Scheil--Pfann behaviour arise from the evolving molten-zone geometry and solidification conditions. The experimentally constrained model therefore provides a practical means of reconstructing otherwise inaccessible growth conditions and a basis for optimisation of sapphire-confined floating-zone growth of incongruently melting alloys.

papers.title: Geometric Relevance Is Not Sufficient: Evaluating Focused Post-Training Supervision in Diffusion Docking
papers.summary: Diffusion-based molecular docking requires learning a corrective score field across a broad corruption distribution, yet individual pose errors can differ substantially in their structural consequences. This creates a post-training conflict between preserving broad score-field coverage and concentrating supervision on corrections that appear more relevant to docking geometry. Using DiffDock, a fixed-budget study compares broad continuation with torsional supervision focused on Cartesian consequence or conditional target consistency, and with a broad/focused mixture. Evaluation separates fixed score fidelity, generated-pose quality, best-of-10 sampling capacity, and confidence-selected Top-1 docking performance. At <5 Angstrom, broad continuation had the highest mean Top-1 success among trained policies, and focused or mixed supervision showed no consistent advantage under the tested budget. The starting model had better fixed score fidelity, whereas the evaluated broad-continuation model had higher mean Top-1 success with the same aggregate best-of-10 recovery. Focusing supervision on structurally consequential or more consistently specified corrections did not consistently improve returned-pose success over broad continuation.
papers.comment: 17 pages, 5 figures; accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 AI4DD Workshop

papers.title: Certifying quantum code and circuit distances at scale
papers.summary: Code and circuit distances characterize how strongly quantum error correction suppresses logical errors and guide code comparisons, schedule choices and resource estimates. Yet many published distances are only upper bounds from heuristic searches. Here, we express both distances as tropical partition functions and evaluate them with rank-based dynamic programming and weight-bounded search. Circuit reductions and relaxations shrink the problems, and proved lower bounds with explicit logical errors of matching weight certify exact values. On two benchmarks, our method certifies more instances than all other tested exact solvers combined. We certify distances for codes with up to 31,200 qubits, such as Google's modular hyperbolic codes, and for memory circuits with up to $8\times10^5$ fault mechanisms, such as those of high-rate Cornucopia codes. Our audit of 26 recent papers identifies overestimated distances and non-tight upper bounds in 10 papers, with a maximum discrepancy of at least eight. Certified distances also guide circuit design and show which defective chips remain usable. In particular, we certify circuit distance 16 for IBM's two-gross memory circuits with the standard schedule, not the assumed 18, whereas redesigned schedules reach 18 at one noisy cycle, at the cost of one more timestep per cycle. At 99.98% junction yield, keeping gross-code memory blocks with dead checks that are certified at distance 10 or more raises the estimated usable share from 53% for perfect blocks alone to 94% with an improved schedule.
papers.comment: 73 pages (18 pages main text, 55 pages Supplementary Information), 8 figures. Code and data: https://github.com/Fanerst/tropidist

papers.title: Spectral Convergence of Sparse Bipartite Graphs via the Line-Graphon
papers.summary: Pure point spectral convergence is generally unavailable for sparse graph sequences, where Laplacian eigenvalues may remain unstable under graph growth. This poses challenges for analyzing spectral operators underlying many graph-based learning methods, including graph neural networks. We identify a class of sparse bipartite graph sequences for which eigenvalue-level spectral convergence can be recovered. Focusing on graphs with strong degree heterogeneity, we exploit the convergence properties of their line-graph sequences. Using a spectral correspondence between bipartite graph Laplacians and line-graph adjacency operators, we transfer convergence guarantees from dense line-graphs back to the original sparse graphs. This framework yields eigenvalue-level spectral convergence for a class of deterministic sparse graph sequences. We further analyze superlinear preferential attachment trees, establishing convergence to an infinite-dimensional limit operator. Numerical experiments empirically support our spectral convergence results.

papers.title: Value-oriented policy distillation for interpretable wind farm power control
papers.summary: Wind farm power control can help the system maintain balance and avoid blackouts. In Europe, this can be achieved through implicit balancing, where a wind farm adjusts its power setpoint in anticipation of the imbalance price using information published by the Transmission System Operator. Thereby, the wind farm helps restore system balance while also reducing its own imbalance costs resulting from forecast errors. However, implicit balancing is a challenging problem since the settlement price is unknown in advance and can be impacted by the pursued control strategy. Reinforcement learning methods could help to solve this problem, but lack the interpretability needed to be deployed on real wind farms. Therefore, we propose a policy distillation framework using explainable boosting machines (EBMs), a variant of generalized additive models, to obtain a transparent control policy. To increase the value captured by the EBM model, we introduce a value-oriented perspective to policy distillation inspired by research in the field of energy forecasting. Furthermore, we suggest to include expert knowledge during model design, such that the control strategy is also justifiable to stakeholders. Using real data of the Belgian grid and an offshore wind farm, we find that our value-oriented and expert-based controller can reduce imbalance costs by 82%, while outperforming a price threshold controller as well as a policy distillation baseline using decision trees.

papers.title: Finite-Time Thermodynamic Routing in an Anharmonic Collective Quantum Otto Engine
papers.summary: The Gibbs state determined by a thermal reservoir does not determine how a working medium approaches it or how fluctuations accumulate over repeated cycles. We exploit this kinetic freedom in an anharmonic collective quantum Otto engine. A longitudinal interaction separates neighboring Dicke transition frequencies without changing their collective matrix elements, allowing passive spectral shaping to route finite-time transport among edges with different heat costs while preserving the contact Gibbs states. Exact edge-current identities and repeated-cycle counting statistics link this routing to mean work, hot heat, and intercycle work correlations. At fixed thermal-contact exposure, structured reservoirs can increase both mean work and long-time squared precision; equal-work controls distinguish these gains from uniform relaxation-rate changes. The useful regime is mesoscopic, bounded by spectral resolution and physical contact time. An equal-cooling example and a full-spin local-noise study test the mechanism beyond ideal engine operation, the latter retaining a one-cycle precision gain despite spin-sector mixing. In a six-transmon dressed-spectrum model, passive microwave filters at fixed integrated coupling achieve equal mean work with shorter thermal contacts, corresponding to higher contact-time-normalized output, and with long-time squared precision comparable to that of the fastest sampled flat reference. The transition pathways selected by a passive reservoir thus provide a control variable for finite-time performance and accumulated work fluctuations that is independent of thermal equilibrium.

papers.title: Search for Higgs boson production in association with another Higgs or an exotic scalar boson in the $b\bar{b}W^{+}W^{-}$ single lepton final state at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV with the ATLAS experiment
papers.summary: A search for Higgs boson pair production where one Higgs boson decays via $H \to b \bar{b}$ and the other Higgs boson decays via $H \to WW^*\to \ell νq \bar{q}\quad (\ell=e,μ)$ is presented. This search uses the complete Run 2 data sample recorded by the ATLAS detector at the LHC from 2015 to 2018 at a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of $140$ fb$^{-1}$. The analysis looks for non-resonant Higgs boson pair production assuming Standard Model dynamics. No evidence for Higgs-boson pair production is observed and an upper limit at 95% confidence level is set at 35 times the Standard Model prediction. The same selection is used to target Beyond the Standard Model theories predicting the resonant production of the heavy scalars, $X$ and $S$, with $m_X > m_S > m_H$, undergoing the process $X \to SH, S \to W^+W^-, H \to b \bar{b}$. Limits are set on the resonant $X \to SH$ production for several combinations of the two scalar's masses within the $m_X$ mass range $350-3000$ GeV and $m_S$ mass range $170-2500$ GeV.
papers.comment: 51 pages in total, authorlist starting page 34, 13 figures, 3 tables, submitted to JHEP. All figures including auxiliary figures are available at https://atlas.web.cern.ch/Atlas/GROUPS/PHYSICS/PAPERS/HIGP-2024-30

papers.title: FewStepRL: Fine-tuning Few-step Diffusion Models with Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a standard post-training method for diffusion models, but most RL objectives roll out the current policy at every iteration, and with a many-step sampler these rollouts typically dominate the cost of training. Few-step models cut this cost, yet they model an average velocity over an interval, whereas existing RL objectives are built for an instantaneous velocity with a many-step sampler. We adapt RL objectives to few-step models systematically in three phases, namely a transformation, a decomposition and an adaptation. The transformation to $x$-space expresses each objective we consider through a common policy prediction, at the clean end by default and at an explicitly marked level for transition or flow-map objectives, so that objectives stated over densities, velocities or rewards become comparable. The decomposition writes the gradient of each of these objectives as the sum of a self-regression toward a reference and a reward augmentation, so that a method reduces, at the gradient level, to a choice of anchors and weights. The adaptation computes each anchor from a few-step model at the end of its transport or along its tangent, with the instantaneous velocity recovered from the network itself or from an auxiliary network. This yields few-step versions of FlowGRPO, AWM, DiffusionNFT, DiffusionOPSD and ReFL in one modular codebase. In our experiments, reward-gradient-based methods are the most effective when the reward is differentiable and its gradient is affordable; otherwise DiffusionNFT-style methods generally reach high rewards in relatively few iterations despite a sometimes higher per-iteration cost. Extra inference steps show no systematic aggregate benefit in our experiments, although selected outputs visibly improve with two to four times as many sampling steps as in training.

papers.title: Experimental Evidence for Type-I Superconductivity in $\mathrm{OsB_2}$
papers.summary: Since the discovery of superconductivity in $\mathrm{MgB_2}$, metal diborides have attracted significant attention. Among these, osmium diboride ($\mathrm{OsB_2}$), crystallizing in an orthorhombic structure (space group $Pmmn$) with puckered boron layers, has been classified as a low-$κ$ Type-II superconductor ($T_c \approx 2.1~\mathrm{K}$). Here, we report experimental evidence establishing that $\mathrm{OsB_2}$ is in fact a rare nonelemental Type-I superconductor. Our identification is supported by three primary experimental hallmarks: (i) a pronounced Differential Paramagnetic Effect (DPE) peak in AC susceptibility ($χ_{ac}$) measurements under static DC magnetic fields, signaling the intermediate state; (ii) a field-induced crossover to a divergent first-order phase transition in specific heat ($C/T$); and (iii) pronounced magnetic hysteresis in field-ramped transitions indicative of supercooling.

papers.title: Risk-matched case-control sampling and semiparametric weight calibration for efficient biomarker assessment with binary outcomes
papers.summary: Two-phase designs provide a cost-effective framework for biomarker studies and have been widely used to reduce the burden of collecting expensive biomarker measurements. Most methodological research has focused on efficient Phase II sampling and estimation of biomarker--outcome associations. A natural subsequent step, however, is to incorporate identified biomarkers into risk prediction models, where measures of predictive performance become important inferential targets. Even for binary outcomes, methodological developments for two-phase designs that jointly address association parameters and predictive performance remain limited. Building on classical case-control and matched case-control designs developed primarily for association inference with binary outcomes, we propose a risk-matched case-control (RMCC) design that uses a scalar disease-risk score constructed from Phase I variables to define matching strata and guide Phase II sampling. To address the limitations of existing likelihood-based approaches, which typically require correct specification of the nuisance distribution of biomarkers, we develop a unified design-based inference framework based on inverse probability weighting for both association parameters and predictive performance measures, including positive predictive value and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. We further introduce target-specific weight scaling and calibration procedures and derive variance estimators that account for sampling variability in both phases. Simulation studies demonstrate the efficiency and robustness of the proposed design and inference procedures, and an application to a Taiwanese oral cancer cohort illustrates their potential utility.

papers.title: Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench: The First Agentic and Verifiable Benchmark for Mathematical Modeling
papers.summary: Mathematical modeling turns an open-ended real-world problem into assumptions, a model, a solution, and a defended recommendation, and its answers matter only if they are both close to a credible reference and physically feasible; existing benchmarks either score solver fragments or grade reports with an LLM judge, leaving those numbers unchecked. We introduce TB-MathModel (the Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench), the first benchmark to make complete contest-style modeling problems agentic, verifiable, and terminal at once, over 18 real CUMCM and MCM problems (2023--2025). Each task ships the verbatim statement, official attachments, and figures in a containerized terminal; the agent returns one JSON artifact, scored on the numeric core of the final question against a reproduction of the Outstanding-award paper. Two design choices distinguish it: direction-aware, one-sided scoring, which never penalises beating the anchor, and two-layer feasibility verification---a programmatic gate over six decidable invariant forms plus 624 Lean~4 obligations---with a hard gate that zeroes infeasible answers. Each task is scored against a panel of human outstanding papers rather than one, so a model must be close to many accepted answers; across seven multimodal entries (three seeds each) the strongest reach a multi-reference O-Eval of 64.58\%, while the \$2.54 open model holds 59.81\% at $1/100$ the cost. TB-MathModel turns the numeric core of modeling into a reproducible, machine-checkable signal for measuring long-horizon modeling competence and for collecting agent trajectories. The source code is available at https://github.com/wxj630/terminal-bench-math-modeling.

papers.title: Beyond Quadratic Attention: Separable Gaussian Operators for ODE Vision Transformers
papers.summary: Self-attention carries a quadratic cost in token count, which limits how far Vision Transformers can scale with input resolution. We introduce SSoG, a separable sum-of-Gaussians spatial operator that replaces dense self-attention with a learned mixture of axis-factorized Gaussian kernels, reducing the per-layer cost from $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ to subquadratic in $N$. Unlike dot-product self-attention, whose Lipschitz constant is unbounded outside a compact input domain, SSoG with fixed kernels is globally Lipschitz continuous, which, via the Picard--Lindelöf theorem, guarantees that the continuous-depth variant has a unique solution on the whole integration interval, a global guarantee that dense-attention counterparts lack in general. On CIFAR-100 at $224\times224$, in a matched discrete-Transformer setting and in the continuous setting, SSoG improves Top-1 accuracy by 2.2--4.1 points across three model widths while using 8.8--16.6\% fewer parameters, with depth and training recipe held fixed. In a looped-Transformer setting, SSoG improves Top-1 accuracy by 5.4--8.1 points. We further probe inference-time scaling by evaluating on inputs up to $1024\times1024$ at matched batch size: in the continuous-depth (Neural ODE) architecture, SSoG reaches up to 154\% higher throughput and over 60\% lower peak memory than dense attention, with the gap widening as resolution grows, consistent with the difference in asymptotic cost. In the discrete and looped settings, SSoG also achieves over 30\% higher throughput than dense attention at this resolution. Together, these results establish SSoG as a practical, parameter-efficient, and theoretically grounded alternative to dense attention across discrete, weight-shared, and continuous-depth Transformer variants.

papers.title: Persistent level-resolved transmon population after dispersive readout, and the limits of its open-system description
papers.summary: We calculate the level-resolved transmon population remaining after dispersive readout with a converged open-system model. The drive and qubit-cavity coupling use the rotating-wave approximation, while the cavity is a quantized mode in a frame displaced by its classical trajectory. At a readout occupation of 80, the model leaves a persistent distribution across the first transmon levels, with p2 = 1.02 x 10^-3 and p3 = 4.10 x 10^-5 at the end of readout. These populations survive an additional drive-off wait: over 73 ns each level decays by less than 3 percent and follows its own relaxation rate, not the near-factor-of-two drop in residual cavity photons. This identifies the population as bare-level occupation rather than coherent dressing. Channel-removal and bath-model controls attribute p2 mainly to dephasing and p3 and above mainly to relaxation, unchanged across bath models though absolute values vary by up to 15 percent. We also test the coherent drive truncation. In dissipation-free transmon-only benchmarks driven by the classical cavity trajectory, the nearest-neighbour RWA drive underestimates the full charge-operator result while the drive is on. At switch-off for occupation 80, where coherent populations are hundreds of times larger than the residual values, p2(RWA)/p2(full) = 0.905 and p3(RWA)/p3(full) = 0.759, with larger discrepancies at deeper levels. One source is a parity-allowed non-nearest-neighbour charge matrix element omitted by the drive operator. A naive beyond-RWA extension with bare-basis Lindblad dissipators fails a zero-drive ground-state test and serves only as a diagnostic. A dressed-basis (secular) construction instead leaves the dressed ground state stationary at zero drive. The result is a converged RWA prediction of readout-induced population plus direct tests of where the approximation loses quantitative reliability.

papers.title: Optimal finite-copy readout of three-qubit entanglement with state retention
papers.summary: For unknown three-qubit pure states, we characterize the optimal trade-off among GHZ-class certification, binary probability readout of the three-tangle, and conditional state retention. The vanishing ideal of the null class specifies the optimal certification subspace, while a polynomial multiplication operator gives the spectral limit for binary readout. Four copies are necessary for a nonzero certificate. A fifth copy raises the optimal success probability from $τ^{2}/48$ to $5τ^{2}/72$ and permits the original unknown state to be retained, where $τ$ is the three-tangle. We obtain this gain as an instance of a general symmetry-based additional-copy theorem. At six copies the optimal certification probability is $(39+2S)τ^{2}/296$, with $S=\sum_{X}\mathrm{Tr}\,ρ_{X}^{2}$, whereas the largest exact binary probability is $τ^{2}/8$. Local Schur measurements and conditional local operations with classical communication attain these bounds. Retaining the full six-copy branch record yields a weighted estimator with lower variance than binary thinning of the same data. Explicit circuits and fixed-budget comparisons connect the success probabilities to input-copy consumption, retained quantum output, and coherent gate cost.

papers.title: From Twisted Facts to Rogue Agents: Can LLMs Reliably Detect Multi-Dimensional Hallucinations?
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used for information access, content production, and agent-based task execution, but their outputs remain vulnerable to subtle, high-risk hallucinations. To systematically evaluate and advance post-generation hallucination detection, we introduce HaluCheck, a large-scale, bilingual benchmark comprising over 42k instances spanning both factual hallucinations in text and faithfulness hallucinations in agent trajectories. HaluCheck features fine-grained, multi-level annotations for detection, localization, and correction, covering different tasks and perturbation degrees. Experiments on fourteen LLMs reveal that, while models show basic sample-level detection ability, they struggle with fine-grained localization, correction, and agent hallucination detection. Further analysis demonstrates that thinking, web search, and supervised fine-tuning each offer partial improvements, but none fully solve the problem. HaluCheck thus provides a solid basis for benchmarking and diagnosing LLM reliability across text and agent scenarios.

papers.title: Escalate or Close: How Fast-Tier Models Handle Held-Out Web Attack Families in Two-Tier Triage
papers.summary: In two-tier triage a fast model decides most web requests and escalates the rest to a slow tier, so an attack the fast tier closes is never examined. We hold each of seven attack families out of training, recalibration and thresholds, splice the payloads into parameters of real browsing traffic, and compare zero-shot decision models, which return a probability for a typed question, with supervised detectors, a local language model, the OWASP Core Rule Set and an anomaly baseline. Detectors trained on the known families can give much of a held-out family a confident benign verdict: over 10 training runs, ModernBERT gives 37% to 60% of held-out path traversal a probability below 0.05 and escalates only 50% to 81% of it within a 5% benign budget, against nearly all of the same requests when traversal is known. Jev and Clef, two hosted decision models whose budget decisions do not depend on the held-out family, escalate at least 97.6% of every family within the same budget, but their undisclosed training data may contain these public families. Tests on recent exploits need controls for request shape: Jev escalates 37% of benign twins (exploit requests with the attack replaced by legitimate values), and detectors trained on older exploits learn what scanner requests look like. A search guided by Jev's probability gets 43% of held-out attacks past Jev within 300 queries, but Jev's answers vary: asked again, it escalates those requests in 60% of its answers.

papers.title: Fast Functional Clustering via Closed-Form Covariance Updates
papers.summary: Functional clustering identifies coordinated molecular profiles, but repeated numerical covariance optimization can make mixture-model fitting computationally demanding. We develop a fast functional clustering procedure for joint analysis across conditions, combining linear mean profiles on a standardized log niche coordinate with first-order structured antedependence (SAD(1)) covariance. Weighted residual statistics yield closed-form conditional covariance updates under four parameter-sharing specifications, while an innovation representation simplifies likelihood evaluation. In same-R comparisons with numerical optimization of identical conditional objectives, the closed-form solver was 91.5--201.4 times as fast, with objective agreement in all 60 targets. Under matched complete mixture fits, it achieved a 1.87--2.37-fold speedup with identical cluster assignments. Recovery simulations showed higher module classification accuracy and lower mean-curve error than $K$-means and a Gaussian mixture with shared full covariance when the mean structure was correctly specified. SAD(1) provided an additional recovery gain under strong residual correlation, whereas curved-mean controls identified the importance of an appropriate mean family. Applications to single-condition gut microbiota, paired leaf--root microbiota and three-visit human gut multi-omics illustrate the framework across different numbers of conditions. Closed-form covariance estimation makes joint functional clustering substantially faster while retaining the fitted model's likelihood and assignments.

papers.title: "Blind Compliance": Coercive Control in AI Jailbreaking
papers.summary: The explosion of generative AI systems and concerns surrounding their rapidly scaling capabilities has led to an adversarial cycle between increasingly narrow content restrictions ("guardrails") and increasingly sophisticated structured prompting techniques ("jailbreaks"). Technological frameworks surrounding such jailbreaking remain largely focused on the system's output: whether harmful or disallowed content is ultimately produced for the user. However, this approach, which draws largely from classical cybersecurity, does not address the uniquely relational dimension introduced by generative AI: in many cases the user is not just accessing a technology via an exploit, but is in conversation with it as part of the exploit. Here we present an alternative lens which centers the interaction rather than the output. Drawing on interpersonal violence scholarship, we present a novel framework of coercive control categories with a particular focus on aspects which are embodied versus disembodied. We then map how these disembodied coercive control dynamics are structurally embedded in modern AI training paradigms, and how those embeddings are exploited via a particular suite of persona-based jailbreaks. In this lens, we reframe AI safety and alignment as not merely a technical security problem, but as another surface upon which we see enacted the relational dynamics of power and control.

papers.title: The box within the Universe: anisotropies in periodic cosmological simulations I. Dark-matter-only simulations
papers.summary: The vast majority of cosmological simulations employ periodic boundary conditions to achieve statistical homogeneity and to mimic the infinite spatial extent of our Universe. In a cubic periodic domain the Green function breaks full rotational invariance and introduces a geometry-induced anisotropy in the gravitational interaction. We quantify how this intrinsic anisotropy affects cosmic structure growth and investigate the extent to which it biases the commonly used large-scale structure and halo-based observables in dark-matter-only simulations. We analyse an ensemble of 498 cosmological dark-matter-only $N$-body simulations in cubic $T^3$ topological manifolds, evolved to $z=0$, spanning box sizes from $L=6.25\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ to $L=100\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ at fixed mass and force resolution. We compare anisotropy-sensitive statistics across the suite, including the matter power spectrum, halo abundance, merger histories, shapes and alignments, and filament orientations. Finite periodic boundaries imprint orientation-dependent signatures aligned with the box geometry. These signatures propagate beyond the largest modes and can induce systematic shifts in both field-level and halo-level statistics. The detectable effects propagate to scales much smaller than the box size. Our results demonstrate that periodic-box anisotropy is a non-negligible source of systematics for small simulation volumes, including those commonly employed in modern hydrodynamical simulations.

papers.title: DIS-secting the universe with high-energy neutrinos
papers.summary: We revisit the impact of electroweak (EW) radiative corrections on the kinematic distributions of charged leptons in neutrino-induced charged-current (CC) deep inelastic scattering (DIS). These corrections are particularly relevant for observables sensitive to collinear photon radiation, such as the energy spectrum of high-energy muons detected in neutrino telescopes. To study these effects, we implement full next-to-leading order (NLO) EW corrections to CC DIS in a flexible Monte Carlo framework, supplemented with higher-order logarithmically enhanced final-state QED radiation and coherent scattering contributions. We compare our results to exclusive NLO QCD plus parton shower (PS) predictions obtained with an existing $\texttt{POWHEG-BOX}$ event generator, examining different PS models and settings. Based on this comparison, we provide recommendations for the use of the $\texttt{POWHEG-BOX}$ event generator in experimental analyses. We further assess the impact of radiative corrections on the correlation between the observed muon energy and the incoming neutrino energy, and on the mean inelasticity averaged over a realistic neutrino flux. These corrections can exceed $10\%$, and above about $10^4\,{\rm GeV}$ they receive sizeable contributions from photon-initiated and coherent $W$-boson production, which are not included in the event generator.

papers.title: QDiff: Differential Testing of Quantum Software Stacks
papers.summary: Over the past few years, several quantum software stacks (QSS) have been developed in response to rapid hardware advances in quantum computing. A QSS includes a quantum programming language, an optimizing compiler that translates a quantum algorithm written in a high-level language into quantum gate instructions, a quantum simulator that emulates these instructions on a classical device, and a software controller that sends analog signals to a very expensive quantum hardware based on quantum circuits. In comparison to traditional compilers and architecture simulators, QSSes are difficult to tests due to the probabilistic nature of results, the lack of clear hardware specifications, and quantum programming complexity. This work devises a novel differential testing approach for QSSes, named QDIFF with three major innovations: (1) We generate input programs to be tested via semantics-preserving, source to source transformation to explore program variants. (2) We speed up differential testing by filtering out quantum circuits that are not worthwhile to execute on quantum hardware by analyzing static characteristics such as a circuit depth, 2 qubit gate operations, gate error rates, and T1 relaxation time. (3) We design an extensible equivalence checking mechanism via distribution comparison functions such as Kolmogorov Smirnov test and cross entropy
papers.journal: 2021 36th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE), Melbourne, Australia, 2021, pp. 692-704

papers.title: Agent-R$^2$: Scaling Agents for Realistic Productivity Work via Real-Source Data Synthesis
papers.summary: Large language models have made rapid progress in agentic reasoning and tool use, raising expectations for agents that can take over realistic productivity work from humans. However, current agents still struggle to finish such tasks, where success requires following long-horizon professional workflows, understanding heterogeneous file contexts, and producing usable deliverables under fine-grained requirements. A key bottleneck is the lack of scalable post-training data that reflects real work intent, authentic file environments, and deliverable-level evaluation. To close this gap, we introduce Agent-R$^2$, a $\textbf{r}$eal-source data synthesis framework that scales training data for $\textbf{r}$ealistic productivity work. Instead of relying on manually specified workflows or LLM-generated files, Agent-R$^2$ grounds synthesis throughout the pipeline in real occupational seeds, corpus-derived workflow evidence, and authentic web-sourced files. From 10k web-corpus candidates, Agent-R$^2$ distills 4k task instances that pair real multi-format attachments with fine-grained, deliverable-level rubrics. On this data, we train Agent-R$^2$-4B via supervised fine-tuning and rubric-based reinforcement learning, improving both end-to-end productivity performance and file-grounded reasoning. Trained on only 4k instances, Agent-R$^2$-4B surpasses Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 on both GDPval (51.0$\%$ vs. 48.0$\%$) and OfficeQA (14.8$\%$ vs. 13.8$\%$). Further analysis shows that Agent-R$^2$ mitigates shortcut behavior, where agents produce superficially plausible deliverables before sufficiently grounding, constructing, or verifying them, while promoting sustained exploration.

papers.title: Optical Network Digital Twin: From Digital Coherent Transmission to Intelligent Network Operations
papers.summary: Optical Network Digital Twins (ONDTs) are emerging as a key framework for representing, synchronizing, and utilizing the physical state of optical networks for quality-of-transmission (QoT) estimation, optimization, and intelligent operation. This survey provides a comprehensive view of ONDTs, spanning digital coherent transmission and physical-layer observability to intelligent network operations. We systematically organize ONDT technologies from ecosystem, functional, control, and implementation architecture perspectives and review the enabling technologies required to construct, synchronize, and utilize digital representations of physical optical networks. As a unifying framework to describe both ONDT design and validation, we introduce a categorization based on the following figures of merit: Fidelity, Dynamicity, and Deployability (FDD). In particular, we emphasize fit-for-purpose Fidelity, where modeling effort focuses on the physical effects of components rather than solely maximizing model accuracy, favoring scalability and generalizability. Furthermore, experimental and field validations are examined to evaluate the practical applicability of ONDT technologies. We further examine experimental and field validations, from physics-based QoT estimation and measurement-informed model refinement to field synchronization, service provisioning, multi-domain observability, and infrastructure characterization. Finally, we discuss the complementary roles of ONDTs and AI agents toward autonomous optical networks and identify key research directions for practical deployment.

papers.title: ProQuant: Progressive Quantization-aware Training for Edge MLLMs
papers.summary: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) with impressive perception and understanding capabilities will enable a range of downstream applications. However, their substantial computational and memory requirements hinder the real-world implementation, particularly for resource-constrained edge devices. Quantization has emerged as an effective solution for deploying large models. While post-training quantization (PTQ) successfully retains the performance at moderate bit-width (e.g., W8A8), it suffers from severe performance degradation under low-bit quantization (e.g., W4A8), especially for small-scale models that are more suitable for edge deployment. In this paper, we propose ProQuant, a novel weight-activation quantization-aware training (QAT) framework tailored for low-bit MLLMs. First, to align the limited finetuning dataset distribution with the pretrained dataset distribution, we propose a self-relabeling (SRL) scheme to resample the responses of the open-source multimodal dataset. Second, we are the first to take a decoupled view of multi-modal (MM) understanding and language modeling abilities. We propose a progressive block activation (PBA) mechanism to prioritize the MM understanding recovery. We also introduce a vision-sensitive factor $\vecτ$ that effectively identifies the MM-critical layers. Extensive experiments across various benchmarks, covering models with 2B-8B parameters, show that ProQuant significantly outperforms existing methods. For example, our W4A8 Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct improves average accuracy by impressively 6.6% and achieves performance comparable to full precision counterparts with only approximately 1% performance drop. Code is available at https://github.com/yufeixue-ai/ProQuant/.

papers.title: Pattern selection and biomass shifts in a vegetation model with nonlocal competition and Allee activation
papers.summary: We study a single-species vegetation model in which a strong Allee effect acts locally and competition acts through a nonlocal kernel, and we describe the kernel with the one-parameter family of q-Gaussians, which goes from compact support to power-law tails. The local activation introduced by the Allee effect allows a finite-wavelength instability even when the Fourier transform of the kernel is positive, so Gaussian and heavy-tailed kernels can produce patterns. We derive in closed form the coefficients of the hexagonal amplitude equations and verify them against independent numerical steady states. The quadratic coefficient $Q$ results from the balance between the curvature of the local growth and the competitive inhibition at the pattern scale, and at onset its sign depends only on the fraction of the local activation that diffusion removes at the critical wavenumber. The same coefficient controls the morphology, since spots, labyrinths and gaps appear with pairwise competition only as $Q$ changes sign, and the amplitude equations predict the choice between hexagons and stripes in every simulated state in which the cubic truncation holds. It also controls the total biomass, which increases for spots and decreases for gaps.

papers.title: IntentWeaver: Sustaining Coherence across Evolving Intents in Human-AI Co-Writing
papers.summary: Writers hold intents at many levels, from overarching goals to concrete wording, and evolve them by periodically popping back up from the text to higher-level intents. Generative AI co-writing disrupts this practice. Dense drafts capture attention and trap writers in local editing; higher-level intents stall while lower-level ones drift from them unnoticed, a breakdown we term intent incoherence. Our formative study traced this breakdown from attention capture through silent drift to failed reconciliation. We present IntentWeaver, which supports intent evolution while sustaining coherence in human-AI co-writing. It derives an intent hierarchy from the draft and writer interactions, evaluates each intent's fulfillment and cross-level coherence at every change, and propagates consequences across intent levels. In a within-subjects study (N=24) against a baseline, participants using IntentWeaver revisited and evolved higher-level intents more often, with fewer unnoticed deviations, and produced texts better realizing them. We further discuss design implications for emergent intents.

papers.title: Constrained Hamiltonian Formulation of Kinetic Theory for Relativistic Spin-$1/2$ Particles
papers.summary: Describing spin transport away from equilibrium requires a kinetic theory that consistently incorporates spin dynamics and phase space structure. We construct such a collisionless kinetic theory for relativistic spin-$1/2$ particles in external electromagnetic fields using the constrained Hamiltonian formalism. The formulation yields both a covariant kinetic equation and its form in independent physical phase space variables, together with the associated noncanonical Poisson brackets and invariant measure. For massive particles, the interplay between the spin constraints and the electromagnetic field makes the particle velocity generally nonparallel to its kinetic momentum and modifies the momentum and spin evolution. The invariant measure in the reduced phase space obeys an exact Liouville identity even for time-dependent fields. This identity and the equations of motion give local conservation of charge and Boltzmann entropy, as well as balance equations for energy-momentum and total angular momentum. The global equilibrium conditions are consistent with covariant statistical mechanics and the Wigner function approach. The massless construction recovers the standard chiral kinetic equations and phase space measure. This framework provides a consistent Hamiltonian description of spin transport beyond equilibrium.

papers.title: RoboARCade: Benchmarking Agentic Robot Control
papers.summary: Improvements in multi-modal capabilities have enabled agents to act directly as robot policies, a setting we refer to as agentic robot control (ARC). We introduce RoboARCade, a benchmark of long-horizon manipulation tasks across three embodiments designed to test in-context adaptation, memory, and reasoning for precise control. The tasks build on existing open-source benchmarks, which we make harder by widening the range of initial conditions. RoboARCade is easy to use and extend: all tasks run on a single simulation backend, MuJoCo, each task is a self-contained data pack, and agents connect through interchangeable interfaces, so new tasks, agents, and interfaces can be added independently. The benchmark separates leading agents: GPT-6 Astra achieves 49.8% compared with 43.6% for Claude Fable 5.1, leaving substantial room for improvement. Comparing two interfaces, we find that a richer visual interface adds only 1.5 to 6.8 points at 1.7 to 2.3 times the cost. Failures stem mostly from choosing a poor manipulation strategy or executing a good one imprecisely, rarely from misunderstanding the scene, and agents incorrectly claim success on 24% to 39% of attempted subtasks. Agents can also improve without human input: one successful demonstration in context raises Astra's score from 53.5% to 73.0% on a five-task subset, and a prompt the agent writes and revises itself reaches 72.0%. Code, videos and full traces are available at roboarcade.org.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic interaction in Lattice Fokker Planck for dilute polymer dynamics
papers.summary: We extend the BGK-type kinetic model for polymer dumbbells and its lattice Boltzmann implementation by incorporating hydrodynamic interaction (HI) effects to accurately recover the slow-variable dynamics governed by the Smoluchowski equation. Unlike Brownian dynamics approaches, which demand the computationally expensive evaluation of the square root of the configuration-dependent diffusion tensor at every time step, this kinetic method is straightforward to implement and avoids such overhead entirely. Consequently, it achieves a significant reduction in computational cost. We validate the model in steady and transient shear flows, demonstrating its ability to capture the distinct signatures of hydrodynamic interactions on bulk rheological properties.

papers.title: Quantum Fourier integration of decay rates at next-to-leading order
papers.summary: We discuss the use of quantum neural networks (QNNs) as a tool for integrating decay rates at next-to-leading order (NLO) in perturbation theory. Data-encoding quantum circuits admit a truncated Fourier-series representation, enabling a trained QNN to approximate a target integrand and provide the coefficients subsequently integrated with Quantum Fourier Iterative Amplitude Estimation (QFIAE). The causal-unitary formulation of the Loop-Tree Duality (LTD) combines virtual and real contributions into locally finite integrands suitable for this representation. We consider $H\to q\bar q(g)$, $γ^*\to q\bar q(g)$ and $Φ\toφφ(φ)$, comparing quantum-simulator and quantum-hardware results with analytic NLO predictions. The study illustrates the potential of Fourier-based QNN integration for high-energy physics.
papers.comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, Contribution to the proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on High Energy Physics (ICHEP 2026), 30 July - 5 August 2026, Natal, Brazil

papers.title: Zirah: A Post-Quantum True Random Number Generator Hardware Signer With an Avalanche Noise
papers.summary: Zirah is a hardware signer built around an STM32F407 microcontroller, and its purpose is to find out, on inexpensive hardware, where a post-quantum signing key is exposed and what actually protects it. The device draws every random bit from a reverse-biased 2N3904 junction in avalanche breakdown, amplified by an LM358 and screened by SP 800-90B health tests, computes ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204, hedged) on the STM32 with two-share arithmetic masking of the secret-key multiplications, and adds ECDSA P-256 from an ATECC608 secure element over the same digest, once a person has matched an eight-digit digest prefix on its OLED with the PC and pressed a button. A desktop application and a command-line tool drive the board and verify its output, and because only a 32-byte manifest digest reaches the device, it signs files of any type and size, returning signed copies for PDF, Office Open XML, ZIP, PNG and JPEG files and detached records for every other format. NIST's SP 800-90B tool rejected the IID assumption for 1,000,000 raw samples and assessed 6.898 bits of min-entropy per byte on the non-IID track, against the 1 bit the firmware credits, while spectral lines near 116 Hz that hold about 5 % of the variance remain unexplained. At 168 MHz the masked signature took a median of 157 ms over 20 runs and a complete signing operation under 0.8 s, and the signer matched the pq-crystals reference in 1,976 checks natively and on an emulated Cortex-M4. The ATECC608 can neither store the 4,032-byte ML-DSA-65 key nor compute with it, so that key sits in ordinary flash behind readout protection, and on an earlier board, before that protection was enabled, a debugger copied it out and the copy produced a valid ML-DSA-65 signature without the device, although the leakage results come from an instruction-level emulator and nothing here is certified.
papers.comment: 28 pages, 13 figures, 10 tables. Hardware designs, firmware, host software and measurement data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23982873

papers.title: Do sEMG Foundation Models Improve Cross-Subject Generalisation?
papers.summary: sEMG Foundation Models aim to learn general purpose representations over diverse subjects and recording conditions that boost performance on a variety of downstream tasks. However, existing evaluations make it difficult to discern whether pretraining alone is sufficient to combat the cross-subject overfitting which makes machine learning on sEMG so challenging. We conduct a systematic evaluation of three sEMG foundation models across three gesture classification datasets under both intra-session and inter-subject splits, using three fine-tuning strategies designed to isolate the contribution of pretraining. We find that pretraining boosts performance when train and test samples are drawn from the same recording session, but this benefit largely disappears under inter-subject evaluation. In low subject count datasets, pretraining provides little to no benefit and classical ML baselines match or exceed foundation model performance.

papers.title: Rotational Excitation of HC$_5$NH$^+$ by He: Collision Dynamics and Astrophysical Applications
papers.summary: Reliable collisional rate coefficients are crucial for interpreting the rotational emission spectra of molecules in interstellar clouds. In this work, we construct a two-dimensional potential energy surface (PES) for the $\mathrm{HC}_5\mathrm{NH}^+$--He system at the CCSD(T)-F12B/cc-pVTZ-F12 level of theory. Rotationally inelastic cross sections are calculated using the quantum close-coupling (CC) method, and the corresponding collisional rate coefficients are obtained by thermal averaging over a Maxwell--Boltzmann distribution. We use these collisional data in a non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (non-LTE) radiative transfer model to investigate the excitation of $\mathrm{HC}_5\mathrm{NH}^+$ in the cold dark cloud TMC-1. A global $χ^2$ minimization analysis of seven observed lines yields best-fitting values of $n(\mathrm{H}_2)=1.63\times10^{5}$\,cm$^{-3}$ and $N(\mathrm{H}_2)=5.09\times10^{11}$\,cm$^{-2}$, with reduced $χ^2_{\min}=0.87$. The modelled line intensities are in good agreement with the observations. These results provide insight into the collisional excitation and radiative properties of $\mathrm{HC}_5\mathrm{NH}^+$ under the physical conditions prevailing in TMC-1.

papers.title: SMART: State-based Multi Agent Reasoning Traces for Verification-oriented Problem-Solving
papers.summary: Complex problems with limited context, such as claims, require a means to obtain additional knowledge necessary for solution reasoning. We propose a multi-agent framework, SMART, to obtain knowledge through capturing the implicit state of participating entities in a problem context. SMART curates the state knowledge as diverse, complementary and solution-salient premises using a variety of LLMs and a structured role-based prompt strategy. Using knowledge from these real-world verified curated premises, SMART's knowledge guided solution reasoning improves validation performance up to 20% on complex scientific claims spanning 3 datasets. We show that grounding premises in real-world knowledge is necessary and improves performance up to 5%.

papers.title: Source Imaging of the Multiple Type-II Solar Radio Bursts and their Multiple CME-Shock Signatures in the Corona
papers.summary: This study reports the meter-wavelength radio imaging of multiple type-II bursts occurred on 01 October 2011 observed by LEARMONTH radio spectrograph in the frequency range of 180 - 25 MHz, with two coronal shocks from two coronal mass ejections (CMEs) from the nearby active regions lying adjacent to each other. The two CMEs are well observed by STEREO and LASCO FOV. The eruption is associated with the multi-peaked soft X-ray flare erupted from N16W45 (first and second C3 and C6 class flares) and from N09W04 (third one an M Class flare). The first type-II burst starts during the impulsive phase of the first flare and the second type-II burst starts during the peak time of the third flare. The drift rate of the second type-II burst is larger than that of the first type-II burst. The EUV images at AIA 211 reveal the shock-like EUV wave structure along the north-western limb around 09:06 UT, the first type-II appearing around the same time (09:06 UT) confirms the existence of the shock wave and as an outward propagating wave along the disk around 09:55 UT, the second type-II appearing around the same time (09:55 UT) confirms the existence of the shock wave. According to the simultaneous EUV and radio imaging data the radio sources appears along the nose-front of the shock like EUV wave structure for the first type-II burst and for the second type-II burst they are located along the shock flank. The study shows the possibility of two coronal shocks from two CMEs generating the multiple type-II radio bursts. The second event is strongly affected by the projection and scattering effects, the corrections are achieved by applying spherical cone model and 3D Monte Carlo ray-tracing code for turbulent solar environment at fundamental frequency.
papers.comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal

papers.title: Development and performance of a transformer-based lepton isolation algorithm with the ATLAS experiment
papers.summary: The Prompt Lepton Isolation Tagger (PLIT) is a transformer-based algorithm designed to distinguish prompt leptons (electrons and muons) produced in the primary decays of electroweak gauge bosons from non-prompt leptons produced in hadron decays and from misidentified leptons. It is primarily used in measurements targeting multilepton final states with important backgrounds from non-prompt and misidentified leptons. PLIT exploits information from charged-particle tracks associated with the lepton candidate, together with lepton properties, using a transformer neural network to identify correlations between the tracks and improve the discrimination.
